summary:
LunaHorizon is an interactive, web-based visualization tool developed to evaluate candidate landing sites on the Moon’s south pole. By translating complex orbital mechanics and NASA topographic data into intuitive, horizon-relative 2D and 3D views, it allows users to instantly track Sun and Earth positions across custom dates.
The challenge of lunar south pole missions lies in extreme lighting and communication constraints, where existing planning tools are often too complex for rapid, collaborative evaluation. LunaHorizon addresses this by calculating local 360-degree horizon masks using NASA LRO LOLA elevation models and SPICE ephemeris kernels. Users can scrub through mission timelines, automatically flag shadowing and communication blackouts, and compare up to three sites side-by-side—switching seamlessly between an Expert Mode for engineers and a simplified Discovery Mode for educators and the public.
This tool is vital because it accelerates landing-zone vetting and reduces mission risk related to power loss and Earth-link blackouts for upcoming Artemis exploration, while simultaneously transforming complex space science into an accessible educational experience.
details:
LunaHorizon is an interactive, web-based visualization and decision-support application designed to simplify the evaluation of candidate landing sites on the Moon’s south pole.
What It Does & How It Works
* Horizon-Relative 3D/2D Visualization: Displays a surface-level perspective of the lunar sky dome, plotting the real-time or time-lapsed paths of the Sun and Earth relative to the surrounding crater rims and ridges.
* Local Horizon-Mask Engine: Ingests high-resolution Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) from NASA’s LRO LOLA instrument and computes a 360-degree elevation profile for any given coordinate. This accounts for local topography that casts long shadows or blocks line-of-sight to Earth.
* Ephemeris & Timeline Scrubbing: Uses NASA NAIF SPICE kernels to calculate precise Sun and Earth azimuth/elevation vectors across multi-year mission windows (e.g., 2026–2030), factoring in lunar libration. Users scrub through a timeline slider to immediately see when solar power drops or communication blackouts occur.
* Side-by-Side Comparison & Scoring: Allows simultaneous comparison of up to three candidate sites (including pre-loaded Artemis III regions), generating a quantitative "Site Viability Score" based on continuous sunlight and Earth-visibility percentages.
Benefits & Intended Impact
* Accelerated Mission Planning: Replaces fragmented command-line scripts and dense tabular outputs with an intuitive visual workspace, allowing science and engineering teams to vet landing zones rapidly and reduce risks of power depletion or lost telemetry.
* Accessible Space Education: Features a dual-tier interface—Expert Mode (raw telemetry, angle readouts, and distribution graphs) for planners, and Discovery Mode (photorealistic LROC terrain overlays and simplified visual sliders) for classrooms and the public—demystifying why future Artemis bases target the lunar poles.
Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software
* Languages: Python (backend data pipeline and orbital math), TypeScript & JavaScript (frontend application logic).
* Frameworks & Libraries: React and Tailwind CSS (UI architecture), Three.js / WebGL (3D sky dome and terrain rendering), Chart.js (illumination and comms timeline graphs), SpiceyPy (NAIF SPICE wrapper), GDAL / Rasterio / Shapely / Pyproj (geospatial DEM processing), and NumPy / SciPy (vector calculations).
* Hardware & Environment: Standard consumer laptops/desktops running modern web browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) for client-side WebGL rendering, paired with a cloud-hosted Python server for heavy raster queries.
Creativity & Key Factors Considered
* Creative Approach: Instead of presenting orbital mechanics from a traditional top-down map view, LunaHorizon shifts the camera to a first-person surface perspective, letting users experience lunar day/night cycles and Earth-rise exactly as a lander’s solar arrays and antennas would. Combining flight-grade SPICE precision with game-engine-style WebGL rendering makes complex astrophysics immediately tangible.
* Factors Considered:
* Extreme Polar Geometry: At ~85°S–90°S, the Sun hovers just degrees above or below the horizon, making millimeter-to-meter terrain accuracy (LOLA DEMs) critical for shadow prediction.
* Lunar Libration: Because Earth oscillates slightly in the lunar sky rather than remaining fixed, exact ephemeris kernels were prioritized over simplified circular orbit approximations.
* Cross-Audience Usability: Balancing technical rigor for aerospace engineers against visual clarity for students without cluttering the interface.
